content.text:
The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "Who believes in an afterlife?": https://pudding.cool/2026/10/lifeafter/
The files: data/height26.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by exploring the data folder and reading the story.

# About this piece
This piece was made by Alvin Chang using data from the Global Flourish Study. The survey data includes nearly 130,000 respondents from 23 countries that completed both waves of the survey in 2022-23 and 2024. The room includes a representative sample of 1,500 respondents. The broad historical and cohort findings are from the Integrated Values Surveys, which combines the World Values Survey and the European Values Study. Percentages are included in the charts, but what drives the findings and the overarching story is the broad comparisons and the direction of change.
One thing that isn’t included in this piece is that the worldwide belief and religiosity numbers have stayed relatively steady. Researchers Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart have found that this is because of two phenomena that cut against each other: One is that people in wealthier countries faced a decreasing amount of existential threats—and, in turn, religiosity and fertility rates dropped. The other is that people in poorer countries still face existential threats, and religion continues to provide security and predictability; fertility rates in those countries have stayed high. As a result, belief has stayed steady worldwide, even though belief within countries has changed rapidly.
The two songs are original compositions, named “Sunday” and “Monday,” created in Ableton Live.
To read more about how this piece was made and to keep up with Alvin’s work, subscribe to this newsletter.

# About this piece
This piece was made by Alvin Chang using data from the Global Flourish Study. The survey data includes nearly 130,000 respondents from 23 countries that completed both waves of the survey in 2022-23 and 2024. The room includes a representative sample of 1,500 respondents. The broad historical and cohort findings are from the Integrated Values Surveys, which combines the World Values Survey and the European Values Study. Percentages are included in the charts, but what drives the findings and the overarching story is the broad comparisons and the direction of change.
One thing that isn’t included in this piece is that the worldwide belief and religiosity numbers have stayed relatively steady. Researchers Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart have found that this is because of two phenomena that cut against each other: One is that people in wealthier countries faced a decreasing amount of existential threats—and, in turn, religiosity and fertility rates dropped. The other is that people in poorer countries still face existential threats, and religion continues to provide security and predictability; fertility rates in those countries have stayed high. As a result, belief has stayed steady worldwide, even though belief within countries has changed rapidly.
The two songs are original compositions, named “Sunday” and “Monday,” created in Ableton Live.
To read more about how this piece was made and to keep up with Alvin’s work, subscribe to this newsletter.

About this piece
This piece was made by
Alvin Chang
using data from the
Global Flourish Study
. The survey data includes nearly 130,000 respondents from 23 countries that completed both waves of the survey in 2022-23 and 2024. The room includes a representative sample of 1,500 respondents. The broad historical and cohort findings are from the
Integrated Values Surveys
, which combines the World Values Survey and the European Values Study. Percentages are included in the charts, but what drives the findings and the overarching story is the broad comparisons and the direction of change.

# About this piece
This piece was made by Alvin Chang using data from the Global Flourish Study. The survey data includes nearly 130,000 respondents from 23 countries that completed both waves of the survey in 2022-23 and 2024. The room includes a representative sample of 1,500 respondents. The broad historical and cohort findings are from the Integrated Values Surveys, which combines the World Values Survey and the European Values Study. Percentages are included in the charts, but what drives the findings and the overarching story is the broad comparisons and the direction of change.
One thing that isn’t included in this piece is that the worldwide belief and religiosity numbers have stayed relatively steady. Researchers Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart have found that this is because of two phenomena that cut against each other: One is that people in wealthier countries faced a decreasing amount of existential threats—and, in turn, religiosity and fertility rates dropped. The other is that people in poorer countries still face existential threats, and religion continues to provide security and predictability; fertility rates in those countries have stayed high. As a result, belief has stayed steady worldwide, even though belief within countries has changed rapidly.
The two songs are original compositions, named “Sunday” and “Monday,” created in Ableton Live.
To read more about how this piece was made and to keep up with Alvin’s work, subscribe to this newsletter.

I’m Alvin Chang, a journalist who tells stories with data and pixels. I’m a Journalism + Design professor at the New School; a data journalist with The Pudding; and the author of a forthcoming book with Riverhead about how we make sense of the world with the maps in our head. More about me here.

In this newsletter I primarily write about map-driven thinking—often related to my work as an educator and visual journalist. As a subscriber, you’ll be the first to be notified about my new projects, often with a behind-the-scenes look at how each piece was created—the inspiration, ideation, and creation.

en-us Mon, 05 Oct 2026 18:36:08 +0000 https://assets.buttondown.email/images/65d4cb4d-5ec0-47df-83ac-898b2d217d0b.png Alvin Chang https://newsletter.alv9n.com Behind the scene: Life After Death? https://newsletter.alv9n.com/archive/life-after-death/

My latest piece is about the afterlife—or at least what humans believe about it. As I write in the piece, what we believe probably doesn't change what happens to us after we die. But it does tell us how we think of our world and our place in it. Go explore the piece, and come back here to read about the thinking behind it.

READ IT HERE »

After grad school, the Boston Globe hired me as a data visualization journalist. I wasn't formally trained in any aspect of the job. The first time I was asked to make a chart, I asked myself: What is the proper way to visualize something?

Now, there are plenty of formalized rules around how to make various chart types, and some rigorous research to back up why we make those decisions. But up to that point in my career, I'd been a reporter and writer, and the process for creating text stories was relatively straightforward:

  1. Gather information

  2. Make sense of the information

  3. Conceptualize a structure to communicate that information

  4. Write the thing

I was particularly interested in points No. 2 and No. 3.

To me, making sense of information is about finding a meaningful structure. As I learn about a topic, my mind starts organizing the information into a sort of map without me even trying. This way of thinking was particularly useful in my new job as a data and visual journalist. Once I understood the information, I tried to draw what was in my head—and then interrogate why I drew it that way. During the nearly two decades of doing this, I couldn't ignore some questions that kept coming up:

Why do we make these pictures in our head to make sense of information? And how do we do it with invisible concepts?

As a writer, I could understand how different strands of information were woven together into meaning. I knew that narrative was a particularly potent tool because it conveyed cause-and-effect quite well—and, when done well, it can also reveal how a system works. When needed, I could also squeeze in some stats to support the piece.

But communicating visually meant that there wasn't always a formalized structure. There was often no inherent order, or embedded denotational meanings. It was merely: What can we put on paper (or the screen) to shoot light rays into people's eyes and, in turn, help them turn that into comprehension about our world? If you've followed my work, you know the winding paths I've taken to explore this question. It's involved unconventional charts, cartoons, videos, and interactive visuals.

In the background, however, I was obsessed with exploring why we (or at least I) make sense of the world spatially and visually.

The last four years, I've been writing a book that explores this question. One thing I've learned is that a growing body of research hints that we organize information in our head—and navigate it—using some of the same neural machinery we use to navigate physical spaces. This makes complete sense; the first thing living creatures have to navigate is their physical environment. It's critical to know where to find food, shelter, and whatever else we need to survive. Humans, of course, need more than just food and shelter—but beyond that, we are capable of constructing and navigating rich constellations of information that help us make sense of our world.

I've filed my manuscript, so hopefully you'll buy the book and read about this obsession sometime next year. But in the meantime, these ideas have infected all my other work, including this piece.

When I first started exploring a story about the afterlife, I immediately had several pictures that popped into my head. Can you tell I grew up in a Protestant household?

But when I thought about who believed in an afterlife and who didn't, I had a tough time understanding how to think about this spatially. If anything, I imagined a bunch of dots visualizing everyone in the world, and a randomized pattern of dots lighting up to represent those who believe.

That's because, in my immediate surroundings, most people don't go around talking about whether they believe in an afterlife or not. We have many identities, religious or otherwise, that are related to beliefs in the afterlife. But beliefs are incredibly personal and volatile—even when it comes to something so big. You could change your mind right now, and there would be no external indication of it.

So I thought: What if we could see what people believed about the afterlife? In fact, what if you could see it when you walk into a room full of people? How would that make you feel about your own beliefs?

And thus was born the idea of creating a room where you could see something that is usually so hidden from us. Not only that, but I wanted to nudge the reader to use their mental mapmaking skills to orient themselves in the room—nonbelievers on the left, unsure people in the middle, believers on the right.

Data visualizations often try to tell the story from an allocentric viewpoint—focusing on the external environment, the bird's eye view, and perhaps helping you place yourself in it. In the case of this room, that means you'd experience it from this map-like layout. But I wanted to combine that with the egocentric view—the experience of walking through the room, not being able to see everyone in the room, but instead running into people with different beliefs. After all, that's how we experience the world!

One thing I didn't want to do was create the sense that these were permanent places in the room—that once you walk in one door, you're basically stuck there. An early version of the room had walls between each section, but I got rid of those to show just how fluid these beliefs can be. I also wanted to show people walking side to side in the room early in the story to further reinforce how no one is permanently stuck there. The only unchangeable thing is how deep they are in the room, since that represents someone's age.

Ultimately, what I hoped to do was give the reader a sense of physical space to represent three invisible things: the inevitable passage of time, an inevitable end, and our agency to explore what comes after. If we really do understand large parts of our world through the maps in our head, then I figured it might be nice to have a thing that represents humanity wrestling with the Big Question—a sort of "social object," to borrow from my former professor, Clay Shirky. (In fact, when I told people I was building this room, it prompted fascinating conversations about where they stand and the journey that brought them there.)

A note on technical learnings: This app uses Three.js, which is a popular Javascript library for creating 3D scenes. My work is usually driven by pixel art—or 2D line art—so I hadn't explored this library too much. But, damn, what a cool library! This project also forced me to finally learn Blender, the 3D modeling tool. To get the variation on the figures, I used a Python script to mess with the models a bit. All this is to say: This is very cool but it's clear that I've built my work on placing pixels on the screen, and not building 3D models. For my next project, I'm thinking of veering into the opposite direction—something very analog, maybe even physical.

My latest piece follows more than 1,000 people as they navigate their love lives across a massive societal disruption—something that has historically exposed the fractures in our relationships. Read it here.

***

I’ve started gravitating toward stories that map of disparate pieces of information. Today’s digital ecosystems deliver tidbits that are hard to piece together into a cohesive model of what’s happening or how the world works. So we end up holding contradictory models that are never resolved, or we end up doubling down on the one that feels most real while angrily rejecting the others. That’s why I find it particularly valuable to go on a journey to map out how everything fits together, and then share that journey with other people.

This story is a prime example of that. It uses the How Couples Meet and Stay Together dataset to track thousands of couples from 2017 to 2022. Much like other longitudinal datasets of that era, the dataset accidentally captures the effects of a global pandemic, and it ends up revealing large-scale shifts in what we think and how we live.

This dataset has probably received most attention from an analysis showing that online dating has become the most common way couples meet. I was able to recreate that analysis using the dataset and included it in my piece, even though that’s not the core of the story.

It’s an astonishing chart that describes a huge shift in human behavior. But when it gets shared on social media, it’s often used to reify our existing beliefs and critiques. This is true of so many social media charts that describe our experiences. They function as Rorschach Tests.

What I tried to do with this piece is show the reader a birds-eye view of more than 1,000 people and what happened to their love lives during and after a global pandemic. Sure, the data is a few years old, but I think we underplay how much it reshaped our world.

In the data, I ended up focusing on something the Stanford researchers found in their 2023 paper: Couples in high-quality relationships were resilient through the stressors of the pandemic, partially because they were able to created shared meaning out of the crisis.

This data story is interesting—and even more so in the historical and academic context of relationships.

For example, it was fascinating to explore what relationships looked like before, why they changed, and what they look like now in this historical context. I read a handful of books for this piece, including Stephanie Coontz’s “Marriage, a History,” which show that our prevailing models of relationships always had tradeoffs and that societal disruptions highlighted the weaknesses in that bargain. Some of these disruptions were bad, like pandemics and economic depressions, and others were driven by technological advancements. (Jean Twenge’s book, “Generations,” argues that the differences in people over time is largely driven by technology. I didn’t include this in the piece, but it’s an interesting thread to pull at.)

I also wanted to add context that helps make sense of the contradictory trend stories we see about relationships. I found a plethora of stories about how the quality of American relationships are eroding and that courting is broken; I also read stories about how American relationships have never been stronger, and that partners rely on each other more than ever. How can both trends be based in data, while existing in the same model of the world? Esther Perel’s “Mating in Captivity,” as well as readings from Eli Finkel, were quite useful. Both of them worried that we’re relying on our partners too much—sometimes to the point of breaking the relationship. And they argue that this is a product of losing the village that used to support our relationships.

I also kept coming back to John Gottman’s “The Science of Trust,” which I read as research for my upcoming book. He describes common traits of successful and unsuccessful relationships.

What I found so powerful about all of this reading is that they help us understand our own experiences, and where they fit into the larger map, both today and across history. # Behind the scene: Life After Death?
2026-10-05
My latest piece is about the afterlife—or at least what humans believe about it. As I write in the piece, what we believe probably doesn't change what happens to us after we die. But it does tell us how we think of our world and our place in it. Go explore the piece, and come back here to read about the thinking behind it.
READ IT HERE »
A small easter egg for those of you reading this: If you right-click and drag up or down in the room, you can fly up and down. (You can also swipe up and down with two fingers on a touch screen.)
After grad school, the Boston Globe hired me as a data visualization journalist. I wasn't formally trained in any aspect of the job. The first time I was asked to make a chart, I asked myself: What is the proper way to visualize something?
Now, there are plenty of formalized rules around how to make various chart types, and some rigorous research to back up why we make those decisions. But up to that point in my career, I'd been a reporter and writer, and the process for creating text stories was relatively straightforward:
- Gather information
- Make sense of the information
- Conceptualize a structure to communicate that information
- Write the thing
I was particularly interested in points No. 2 and No. 3.
To me, making sense of information is about finding a meaningful structure. As I learn about a topic, my mind starts organizing the information into a sort of map without me even trying. This way of thinking was particularly useful in my new job as a data and visual journalist. Once I understood the information, I tried to draw what was in my head—and then interrogate why I drew it that way. During the nearly two decades of doing this, I couldn't ignore some questions that kept coming up:
Why do we make these pictures in our head to make sense of information? And how do we do it with invisible concepts?
As a writer, I could understand how different strands of information were woven together into meaning. I knew that narrative was a particularly potent tool because it conveyed cause-and-effect quite well—and, when done well, it can also reveal how a system works. When needed, I could also squeeze in some stats to support the piece.
But communicating visually meant that there wasn't always a formalized structure. There was often no inherent order, or embedded denotational meanings. It was merely: What can we put on paper (or the screen) to shoot light rays into people's eyes and, in turn, help them turn that into comprehension about our world? If you've followed my work, you know the winding paths I've taken to explore this question. It's involved unconventional charts, cartoons, videos, and interactive visuals.
In the background, however, I was obsessed with exploring why we (or at least I) make sense of the world spatially and visually.
The last four years, I've been writing a book that explores this question. One thing I've learned is that a growing body of research hints that we organize information in our head—and navigate it—using some of the same neural machinery we use to navigate physical spaces. This makes complete sense; the first thing living creatures have to navigate is their physical environment. It's critical to know where to find food, shelter, and whatever else we need to survive. Humans, of course, need more than just food and shelter—but beyond that, we are capable of constructing and navigating rich constellations of information that help us make sense of our world.
I've filed my manuscript, so hopefully you'll buy the book and read about this obsession sometime next year. But in the meantime, these ideas have infected all my other work, including this piece.
When I first started exploring a story about the afterlife , I immediately had several pictures that popped into my head. Can you tell I grew up in a Protestant household?
When I was a toddler, the only VHS tape my family owned was the Disney film "Dumbo," which depicts babies coming from the sky—somewhere above the clouds.
Dante wrote that hell was below and heaven was above—and that we were, well, here. (Image from Filippo Giunta’s woodcut illustration)
Saint Peter at the gates of heaven—and that other guy who the Bible forgot to mention. (From the New Yorker)
But when I thought about who believed in an afterlife and who didn't, I had a tough time understanding how to think about this spatially. If anything, I imagined a bunch of dots visualizing everyone in the world, and a randomized pattern of dots lighting up to represent those who believe.
Anyone else have a Lite-Brite growing up?
That's because, in my immediate surroundings, most people don't go around talking about whether they believe in an afterlife or not. We have many identities, religious or otherwise, that are related to beliefs in the afterlife. But beliefs are incredibly personal and volatile—even when it comes to something so big. You could change your mind right now, and there would be no external indication of it.
So I thought: What if we could see what people believed about the afterlife? In fact, what if you could see it when you walk into a room full of people? How would that make you feel about your own beliefs?
And thus was born the idea of creating a room where you could see something that is usually so hidden from us. Not only that, but I wanted to nudge the reader to use their mental mapmaking skills to orient themselves in the room—nonbelievers on the left, unsure people in the middle, believers on the right.
A very early sketch of the room layout. I eventually got rid of the foyer because who can afford a foyer in this economy?
Data visualizations often try to tell the story from an allocentric viewpoint—focusing on the external environment, the bird's eye view, and perhaps helping you place yourself in it. In the case of this room, that means you'd experience it from this map-like layout. But I wanted to combine that with the egocentric view—the experience of walking through the room, not being able to see everyone in the room, but instead running into people with different beliefs. After all, that's how we experience the world!
An early sketch in which I ask, "What is beyond the end?" You'll have to read the piece to find out.
One thing I didn't want to do was create the sense that these were permanent places in the room—that once you walk in one door, you're basically stuck there. An early version of the room had walls between each section, but I got rid of those to show just how fluid these beliefs can be. I also wanted to show people walking side to side in the room early in the story to further reinforce how no one is permanently stuck there. The only unchangeable thing is how deep they are in the room, since that represents someone's age.
Ultimately, what I hoped to do was give the reader a sense of physical space to represent three invisible things: the inevitable passage of time, an inevitable end, and our agency to explore what comes after. If we really do understand large parts of our world through the maps in our head, then I figured it might be nice to have a thing that represents humanity wrestling with the Big Question—a sort of "social object," to borrow from my former professor, Clay Shirky. (In fact, when I told people I was building this room, it prompted fascinating conversations about where they stand and the journey that brought them there.)
A note on technical learnings: This app uses Three.js, which is a popular Javascript library for creating 3D scenes. My work is usually driven by pixel art—or 2D line art—so I hadn't explored this library too much. But, damn, what a cool library! This project also forced me to finally learn Blender, the 3D modeling tool. To get the variation on the figures, I used a Python script to mess with the models a bit. All this is to say: This is very cool but it's clear that I've built my work on placing pixels on the screen, and not building 3D models. For my next project, I'm thinking of veering into the opposite direction—something very analog, maybe even physical.

# About this piece
This piece was made by Alvin Chang using data from the Global Flourish Study. The survey data includes nearly 130,000 respondents from 23 countries that completed both waves of the survey in 2022-23 and 2024. The room includes a representative sample of 1,500 respondents. The broad historical and cohort findings are from the Integrated Values Surveys, which combines the World Values Survey and the European Values Study. Percentages are included in the charts, but what drives the findings and the overarching story is the broad comparisons and the direction of change.
One thing that isn’t included in this piece is that the worldwide belief and religiosity numbers have stayed relatively steady. Researchers Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart have found that this is because of two phenomena that cut against each other: One is that people in wealthier countries faced a decreasing amount of existential threats—and, in turn, religiosity and fertility rates dropped. The other is that people in poorer countries still face existential threats, and religion continues to provide security and predictability; fertility rates in those countries have stayed high. As a result, belief has stayed steady worldwide, even though belief within countries has changed rapidly.
The two songs are original compositions, named “Sunday” and “Monday,” created in Ableton Live.
To read more about how this piece was made and to keep up with Alvin’s work, subscribe to this newsletter.

The broad historical and cohort findings are from the [Integrated Values Surveys](https://www.worldvaluessurvey.org/WVSNewsShow.jsp?ID=442), which combines the World Values Survey and the European Values Study. Percentages are included in the charts, but what drives the findings and the overarching story is the broad comparisons and the direction of change.\r
\r

One thing that isn’t included in this piece is that the worldwide belief and religiosity numbers have stayed relatively steady. Researchers Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart have [found](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/sacred-and-secular/5CE209CE245D444D40BB44D0DDD78F43) that this is because of two phenomena that cut against each other: One is that people in wealthier countries faced a decreasing amount of existential threats—and, in turn, religiosity and fertility rates dropped. The other is that people in poorer countries still face existential threats, and religion continues to provide security and predictability; fertility rates in those countries have stayed high. As a result, belief has stayed steady worldwide, even though belief within countries has changed rapidly.\r
\r
\r
The two songs are original compositions, named “Sunday” and “Monday,” created in Ableton Live.\r
